title: Big Tech Books $160 Billion in Paper Gains From AI Investment Stakes
excerpt: Alphabet and Amazon posted record quarterly profits, but much of the surge came from unrealized valuation gains on equity stakes in companies like Anthropic and SpaceX rather than core business revenue.
body:
• Big Tech companies booked over $160 billion in combined profit boosts from valuation gains on equity stakes in AI companies during Q2 2026, according to the Financial Times.
  • Alphabet's net income tripled to $112 billion, with roughly $99 billion from unrealized gains on SpaceX and Anthropic holdings — none of it cash.
  • Amazon reported $53.4 billion in non-operating income, primarily from a $50.5 billion upward adjustment on its Anthropic preferred stock.
  • Analysts warn of a "circular financing" dynamic in which cloud giants invest in AI labs that spend heavily on cloud services, inflating paper profits on both sides.

The largest U.S. technology companies collectively booked more than $160 billion in profit boosts during the second quarter of 2026 from valuation gains on their stakes in artificial intelligence companies, according to the Financial Times — a figure that has prompted Wall Street analysts to question the quality of Big Tech's record earnings.

Alphabet and Amazon led the surge. Alphabet reported net income of $112.11 billion for the quarter ended June 30, roughly triple the $28.2 billion it earned a year earlier, according to Fortune. But the headline number obscured a critical detail: the company booked just over $99 billion in gains on equity securities, mostly unrealized, tied primarily to its holdings in SpaceX and Anthropic.

Paper Gains, Not Cash

The SpaceX gains became visible after the rocket company's IPO in June. The Information reported that Alphabet disclosed $94.1 billion in SpaceX shares, representing about 6% of the company. A portion of those shares are restricted from short-term sale, and another $14.1 billion remains locked up through the third quarter of 2027.

Amazon told a parallel story centered on Anthropic. In its SEC filing, Amazon said net income rose to $62.6 billion, with $53.4 billion of that coming from non-operating pre-tax income — primarily its Anthropic investments. The company recorded approximately $50.5 billion in upward adjustments to its Anthropic nonvoting preferred stock following observable changes in price from the AI company's latest funding rounds.

"The hyperscalers' earnings growth this quarter was boosted by an unusually large contribution from equity stakes in private companies."

— Goldman Sachs Research Note

Goldman Sachs analysts found that 34% of the profit earned by the five largest cloud computing and platform providers — Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, and Oracle — was attributable to "other income" in the quarter, the highest such share in at least a decade. Some $49 billion of that was explicitly connected to equity stakes in private companies, according to the Times.

The Circular AI Economy

The profit dynamics have raised concerns about what analysts have termed "circular financing" in the AI sector. Cloud giants invest billions in AI model companies. Those same AI companies then commit massive sums back to the cloud platforms: Anthropic signed a $200 billion, five-year commitment with Google Cloud in May and a $100 billion deal with Amazon Web Services in April, according to the Times.

Anthropic and OpenAI together now account for roughly half of the cloud computing order backlog at Oracle, Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft, the Information reported. The interdependence means that rising private valuations create paper gains for investors who are also the primary revenue source for the companies they are investing in.

IPOs Will Test the Valuations

The stakes are about to get a market reality check. Anthropic raised $65 billion in Series H funding in May at a $965 billion post-money valuation, with Altimeter Capital, Sequoia Capital, and others leading the round. Its revenue run rate crossed $47 billion that month and reached $65 billion by the end of July, according to Bloomberg reporting republished by the Los Angeles Times.

Axios reported that Anthropic filed confidential IPO papers with the SEC in June, while OpenAI was also preparing a confidential prospectus. If both AI labs come to market around the same window, investors will have to compare revenue quality, compute costs, and cloud obligations head-on.

"If both companies come to market around the same window, investors won't be judging AI labs in isolation. They'll compare revenue quality, compute costs, and how much of the boom is being financed by the same small group of partners."

— Startup Fortune

The risk for Big Tech is straightforward: if Anthropic or OpenAI list below their latest private valuations, the same balance sheets that booked upward adjustments will be forced to record write-downs. Amazon's SEC filing shows how large the exposure has become — it now holds Anthropic preferred shares and convertible notes whose values depend heavily on where the next real price lands.

The Spending Does Not Stop

Meanwhile, the capital expenditure race shows no sign of slowing. The five largest hyperscalers have guided for a combined $700 billion or more in AI-related capex for 2026, according to Morningstar: $200 billion for Amazon, up to $190 billion each for Microsoft and Alphabet, up to $145 billion for Meta, and $50 billion for Oracle. Gary Marcus, the AI researcher, called this spending "the greatest capital misallocation in history."

Alphabet's core search business and Amazon's AWS remain massive cash generators. Nobody is arguing that these are weak companies. The question is whether a quarter in which paper mark-ups account for the majority of headline profits is telling investors the same story as actual revenue growth — and whether the AI boom's circular economics can survive contact with public markets.
